newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan calls for peace with India on jubilee.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan calls for peace with India on jubilee.

text.p: Amid fireworks and flags, Pakistan ushered in its 50th anniversary of independence on Thursday, with Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif calling for peace with India and a solution to the Kashmir conflict.

In a speech at a flag-raising ceremony in Islamabad, he said Pakistan had initiated a dialogue with India because of what he called a growing realisation on both sides that the bitter 50-year-old Kashmir dispute should be resolved.

"The...conflict and arms race between the two countries wasted billions of dollars," he said. "It also deprived the peoples of the two countries of peace and prosperity. The interests of both India and Pakistan were hurt...

"I hope that India would also respond with the same sincerity by withdrawing its forces from occupied Kashmir and putting an end to atrocities there and hence pave the way for establishment of lasting peace in the region," he declared.
In a speech to the National Assembly (lower house) at one minute past midnight, Sharif praised Kashmiris fighting Indian troops in the two-thirds of Kashmir under New Delhi's control.
"Today mujahideen (guerrillas) are fighting for their independence in occupied Kashmir. God willing, the Kashmiri people will fulfil their mission one day," he said.
"Pakistan will continue to provide moral support to them. Our independence will be complete on the day all our Kashmiri brethren join us in celebrating independence."

Pakistan, which holds one-third of the Himalayan region, denies Indian accusations that it arms, trains and finances the Kashmiri guerrillas, whose insurgency has cost an estimated 20,000 lives since it erupted in 1990.
Sharif, who swept to power after February elections, said Pakistan should set aside political bitterness and urged the opposition to help start a new era of development and progress.
He was speaking only hours after Benazir Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party walked out of parliamentary sessions at which the government pushed through a sweeping new anti-terrorism act.

The act, which needs only presidential assent to become law, is designed to combat a wave of violence involving Sunni and Shi'ite militants in the populous province of Punjab, as well as ethnic unrest in the southern port city of Karachi.

Despite their country's economic and political woes, many ordinary Pakistanis took to the streets at midnight to let off firecrackers and cheer the anniversary of August 14, 1947, when Pakistan and India won their independence from British rule.
Sharif's brother, Punjab province chief minister Shahbaz Sharif, led a big rally in the city of Rawalpindi, near the capital Islamabad, with a fireworks display after midnight.

After the flag-raising in Islamabad, the prime minister flew to Lahore where he laid a wreath at the memorial to national poet Allama Iqbal. He was due to fly to Karachi for an evening rally at the mausoleum of Pakistan's founder Mohammad Ali Jinnah, always referred to here as Qaid-e-Azam (great leader).

Official celebrations were low-key, with no military parades or lavish events, reflecting a mood of introspection and austerity in a country grappling with sectarian violence and searching for a way out of a chronic economic crisis.

"State institutions and the infrastructure are crumbling, lawlessness threatens society, the debt trap is daunting and the economy is in dire straits," the English-language daily The News said in an editorial on Thursday. "Government credibility and faith in its ability to turn things around is very low."

"Despite the general cynicism and despondency that overshadow the celebrations...Pakistan is not about to collapse," the newspaper said. "It is inherently viable and vibrant enough to belie those who declare it a failed state."
